ideas.title: Hot-Hand Lineage: How Much Is Inherited?
ideas.pitch: Interactive binary lineage tree where each 'cell' is a team/player with a fate (win-streak vs slump). Slide a heritability dial from 0 (every fate an independent coin flip) to 1 (fate copied from parent). The page computes an inheritance-entropy-style score (how much a node's fate is predicted by its ancestors, model-independent) live. Try to guess the dial from the tree alone, then see the score. Teaches whether momentum or hot hands are real or just heterogeneity.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatability: 'is momentum real?' is a classic sports and betting fight. Fit: streak and hot-hand modeling. Surprise: heterogeneity can fake heredity. Whimsy: guess-the-dial game. Votes empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Momentum Entropy: Model-Free Streak Inheritance Test for Bettors
ideas.pitch: Port inheritance entropy to game sequences. Treat a team's season as a lineage tree (game to next game, split by home/away or opponent type) and measure how much outcome info carries forward without assuming a model like Elo or a Markov chain. Run it across NBA/NFL logs from SharpLab to find which teams or leagues have real carryover and which are noise, then flag bet-relevant regime persistence.
ideas.discussion_why: Directly on point for betting debates (momentum, rest, regression). Model-independent claim invites argument. Moderate surprise. Votes empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Your Poker Reads Are a Sparse Connectivity Problem
ideas.pitch: Video explainer: recovering a hidden network's weights from only partial observations by accumulating pairwise covariances across sessions, then pruning with Granger causality. Analogy: you only see some players per table each night, yet reconstruct who influences whom (tilt contagion, follow-the-leader betting). Animate covariance accumulation filling in a sparse matrix as sessions stack.
ideas.discussion_why: Fun analogy to table dynamics and sharp-money copying. Moderate fit, mild surprise that partial views suffice. Votes empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Casino Hash Table: Watch Quadratic Probing Choke at 99% Full
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML where a hash table is a casino floor of slot machines (buckets). Drag a load-factor slider toward 1-eps and watch keys 'gamble' for an open seat via quadratic probing (h+i^2). A live histogram of probes per insertion is plotted against the eps^-(1+o(1)) curve from the paper, next to linear probing (~1/eps^2) and ideal random probing (~(1/eps)ln(1/eps)). Add a 'Play as a key' mode where you pick probe offsets and race the algorithm. The point is to feel the 1968 conjecture: near-full tables cost about 1/eps tries, not 1/eps^2.
ideas.discussion_why: Fit is moderate: 'finding an open seat' maps to waiting-for-a-seat and geometric-trials intuition. Surprise is real, since a 58-year-old conjecture finally got near-optimal. Whimsy is high from the casino-floor theming. Votes were empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Isotonic Prop Surrogate: Monotone Emulator for Expensive Sports Sims
ideas.pitch: Many betting models are expensive simulators (full-game Monte Carlo, lineup/minutes sims) with many inputs: pace, minutes, usage, spread, rest. Their outputs are monotone in most inputs: more minutes means more rebounds, bigger spread means higher blowout probability. Use the paper's Bayesian isotonic surrogate to emulate the sim from a few hundred runs, with no shape misspecification and calibrated uncertainty. That gives instant line-shopping across thousands of what-if scenarios. Ship it as a Discord /whatif command: 'what if Jokic gets 4 fewer minutes?' returns a posterior band on the prop mean. It plugs into the existing nba-props terminal as a fast surrogate over the GR-RTRMC-completed player matrix, with monotonicity constraints as a free sanity prior.
ideas.discussion_why: Strong betting and sports fit, and the 'what-if' command is something people would use and argue over: do monotonic priors beat flexible ML on props? The surprise is moderate. Whimsy is low. Votes were empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Why 'Just Pool the Bankroll' Is the Oldest Con in Gambling (DeFi Vaults Explained)
ideas.pitch: Walk through the DeFi vault SoK (pooled deposits, tokenized shares, curator control layers) as a staking-horse and poker-backing story. A vault is a backing marketplace where the curator is the horse, the shares are makeup-tracking tokens, and the strategy contract is the bankroll rules. Cover the failure modes (curator discretion, share-price manipulation, withdrawal runs) and compare them to real poker staking disputes and fund-of-funds blowups. Close with a design checklist: what a trustless poker-staking vault would need so makeup can't be fudged.
ideas.discussion_why: Poker staking and backing is a topic people already argue about, and it ties to gambling and decision-theory directly. The surprise is that DeFi rebuilt the staking problem. Whimsy is moderate. Votes were empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: How Many Stats Can One Neuron Read? Linear Decoder Capacity Toy
ideas.pitch: Interactive toy based on the regression-capacity theory: a 'scout brain' (N noisy neurons) must linearly read P continuous variables (speed, vision, clutch, and so on) from manifold-shaped responses. Sliders for N, P, manifold radius and dimension show the sharp phase transition where the linear readout stops fitting. Reframe it as 'how many player attributes can one linear scouting model decode before it fails?' with the capacity curve drawn live from random-data simulation. The takeaway is the overfitting cliff at roughly P/N, and how manifold geometry shifts it.
ideas.discussion_why: The sports-scouting analogy is a stretch, but the phase-transition cliff is surprising and visual. Betting fit is modest, and it appeals to the modeling crowd who debate overfitting in player props. Votes were empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Quon Table: Deal Cards Between Bosons and Fermions
ideas.pitch: Quons interpolate between bosons (q=1) and fermions (q=-1) via a parameter q. Single-file HTML where a slider sets q and you watch particles fill seats at a poker table. At q=-1 no two share a seat (Pauli, like a no-duplicate deck deal). At q=1 they pile on the same seat (like with-replacement draws). In between, the occupancy probabilities follow the quon q-deformed counting weights. Simulate thousands of 'hands' and plot the distribution of how many identical cards show up, so you can feel the continuum from sampling without replacement to sampling with replacement.
ideas.discussion_why: Fits poker/cards well, since dealing without versus with replacement is a familiar intuition. 'Wait, there's a dial between them?' gives surprise, and the quon framing is whimsical. votes.json is empty, so no tag bias was applied.

ideas.title: Market Ecology Sim: Many RL Bettors vs a Reactive Book
ideas.pitch: Adapt the three-trophic-level agent-based market model (learning agents, liquidity takers, market makers) to a sports betting exchange or prop market. Several RL bettors that must unwind or execute large stakes interact with a reactive market-maker book. Impact emerges rather than being hard-coded. Test how many RL syndicates it takes before everyone's edge on a thin NBA prop line is arbitraged away, and how line movement and CLV decay as agents are added. This plugs into SharpLab's CLV tracking as a stress-test sandbox.
ideas.discussion_why: Betting-market structure and 'how many sharps kill an edge' are things the server cares about, and emergent market impact from competing bots is a surprising result. Fits betting, sports and decision theory. No vote bias applied because votes.json is empty.

ideas.title: Is Your Sharp Friend's Tip Actually Informative? The Reflection Problem in Betting Herds
ideas.pitch: Video explainer on the linear-in-means reflection problem. If you bet like your friends, you can't tell whether they influence you or you influence them. Friends-of-friends instruments are supposed to fix this, but the paper shows they're usually weak in real networks. Walk through a Discord betting-server example where everyone tails the same capper, show why naive 'peer effect' estimates are biased, and run a simulation where the weak-instrument F-statistic collapses on realistic sparse graphs.
ideas.discussion_why: Herd-betting and tailing are very relatable, and 'you can't tell who influenced whom' is a counterintuitive claim. It fits betting and decision theory, with a bit of econometrics nerdiness. No vote bias applied because votes.json is empty.

ideas.title: p-adic Dice: A Game Where Close Means Divisible
ideas.pitch: In Q_p, two numbers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of p, and the space is totally disconnected, so a loss is flat away from the minimum. Build a guessing game where you hunt for a hidden number and the feedback is only the p-adic distance (how many trailing digits in base p match). Players feel why naive gradient descent fails: the landscape is a staircase of plateaus. Then toggle a continuous relaxation, as in the paper, that smooths the digits so you can descend. The page shows a tree of digit-prefix nodes lighting up as you home in, and you can race against the bot.
ideas.discussion_why: It's a guessing game with weird feedback, so it fits games and whimsy, and 'closeness is divisibility' surprises people. It has less direct betting relevance. No vote bias applied because votes.json is empty.

ideas.title: Tail-Risk Bankroll Bot Tournament (CVaR vs Mean Selection)
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML: evolve a population of betting/poker bankroll strategies (bet fraction, stop-loss, tilt threshold) over simulated fat-tailed sessions. Toggle the selection rule between mean ROI and CVaR(5%), per CVaR-RMD. Mean selection breeds degenerate over-bettors that look great until a rare blowup wipes them. CVaR selection breeds boring survivors. Live histogram of each generation's loss tail, plus a 'run 1000 fresh seasons' button that reveals the hidden ruin rate of the mean-selected champion.
ideas.discussion_why: High relatability (every bettor has been wrecked by a 'profitable' system), strong decision-theory and gambling fit, and a surprising reveal that the best average strategy is the one that blows up. The evolving-bots angle adds whimsy. No votes recorded yet, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: No-Trade Band Bankroll Rebalancer
ideas.pitch: Interactive CRRA bankroll sim: you hold a Kelly-style fraction in a repeated +EV bet stream, but every rebalance costs a fee (vig or slippage). Drag the cost slider and watch the paper's leading-order no-trade band widen, with a width that scales like cost^(1/3) as the singular perturbation result implies. Race 'rebalance constantly' against 'only act outside the band' on the same random paths and compare final wealth. Includes a risk-aversion (gamma) knob.
ideas.discussion_why: The surprising claim is that doing nothing most of the time beats constant adjusting. It maps directly onto Kelly sizing, vig, and when to re-bet or hedge, and it will split the room between full-Kelly and fractional-Kelly camps. No votes recorded yet, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Your Betting Model Is Evaluated on the Wrong Metric
ideas.pitch: A video essay on mean versus tail selection. Cover how CVaR-RMD finds that LLM-discovered heuristics selected by average score hide rare severe failures. Draw the parallel to sportsbook model backtests ranked by ROI, poker players ranked by winrate, and parlay hunters. Use three case studies with simulated equity curves and show CVaR(5%) rankings flipping the leaderboard. End with a lesson on picking strategies by worst-5% outcomes.
ideas.discussion_why: It challenges the standard way bettors judge systems (ROI, winrate) and ties poker variance to a concrete tail-risk metric. It will draw debate about risk of ruin versus EV. No votes recorded yet, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Unavoidable Pattern: Can You 2-Color Your Way Out?
ideas.pitch: Interactive toy built on vertex-Ramsey classes. Pick a small graph H (triangle, path, star, C5) and a host graph G, then try to k-color G's vertices to avoid a monochromatic induced copy of H. A solver reveals whether G forces H. The paper's result is that the set of forcing graphs is a fingerprint, since non-isomorphic H never share the same class. The demo shows two different H's with a host that forces one but not the other, so you can see that distinct graphs have distinct forcing sets. Framed as a game: you play the colorer against a pattern-detector.
ideas.discussion_why: Mostly surprise and whimsy. A coloring puzzle fits games, and 'you can't dodge the pattern' is a Ramsey-style hook. It has little direct betting relevance, and votes.json is empty so no bias was applied.

ideas.title: Your Betting Streaks Are Forced: Ramsey Theory and the Hot Hand
ideas.pitch: Video explainer. Any k-coloring of a big enough structure must contain a monochromatic induced copy of H, and the paper adds that the set of such forcing graphs uniquely identifies H. Apply it to win/loss sequences and lineup or matchup graphs: in a dense enough schedule graph, 'streaky' substructures are mathematically guaranteed no matter how outcomes are assigned. The video then asks which streaks are pure combinatorics and which are real signal, which is the hot-hand debate seen through Ramsey.
ideas.discussion_why: The hot-hand and streak debate is very relatable to a betting and sports crowd. 'Streaks are guaranteed by math' is a surprising claim, and it fits sports and decision-theory. The Ramsey-to-sports stretch will draw pushback, which helps debate. No vote bias applied since votes.json is empty.

ideas.title: Rough-Edge Smoothing: Plastic Flattening as a Model of Line Movement
ideas.pitch: Treat a market's price surface (odds across books, or the order book) as a rough surface. Sharp asperities (stale or mispriced lines) get plastically flattened under pressure from sharp money, as in the squeezed-metal-block model, where the contact area grows and the peaks yield first. Build a toy simulator that squeezes a rough odds profile with 'load' (volume) and tracks how fast the arbitrage roughness (RMS spread across books) decays. Then fit the decay curve to real multi-book NBA lines in SharpLab to estimate how load predicts how quickly a stale line closes.
ideas.discussion_why: The analogy is weird and delightful: market efficiency as metal being squeezed. It maps onto betting, since stale-line decay and closing-line value are live topics. The fit is speculative, so it will draw debate. No vote bias applied since votes.json is empty.

ideas.title: Spend Your Rights: Multi-Stop Put Lab
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML. A CRR binomial tree price path plays out step by step. You hold k exercise rights on an American put and must choose when to cash each one. A recursive Snell-envelope solver (V_k = max(payoff + V_{k-1}, continuation)) runs alongside and shows the optimal stopping boundary for each remaining right. Score yourself against the optimal policy. Slider for k, up/down probability, and strike. Toggle to the Russian option (running-max payoff) to see the boundary change. It is a feel-it explainer for the paper's point that unused rights change the value of the one you're holding.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatable to betting and poker: cash out now or wait, with several chips left to spend. It is the same logic as hedging or cashing out a parlay leg. The surprise is that the optimal threshold for your first exercise moves depending on how many rights remain. Votes file was empty, so no tag bias was applied.

ideas.title: When Should You Cash Out? Optimal Stopping With Several Bullets
ideas.pitch: A video that starts with a cash-out button on a live bet, then builds the Snell envelope on a coin-flip random walk. It then adds the multiple-stopping twist: you get 3 cash-outs per season (3 parlay hedges, 3 re-buys, 3 fold-equity bluffs). The recursion shows that the value of the last right is the single-stop price, and each earlier right is that price plus a continuation correction. The video ends with a comparison of greedy play and the optimal policy on simulated paths.
ideas.discussion_why: A cash-out-or-ride debate is native to a betting server. Everyone has a strong opinion on hedging, and the video gives them a math answer to argue with. The medium-high surprise comes from limited-use options having non-obvious thresholds.

ideas.title: Limited-Hedge Optimizer for Live Betting
ideas.pitch: A Discord bot where you give it a live-win-probability random walk model (for example, an NBA win-prob path discretized to a binomial tree) and a budget of N cash-out or hedge rights for the night or the game. It computes the multiple-stopping optimal policy through recursive Snell envelopes and answers 'cash out now or hold?' per bet. Backtest against logged SharpLab live odds to see whether hedge timing adds CLV or only reduces variance.
ideas.discussion_why: Directly about betting: it puts a number on hedging, a recurring argument. Whether hedging is +EV or just variance reduction will split the room. Fits the existing SharpLab stack.

ideas.title: Spoofed! GPS Pseudorange Detective Game
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML puzzle. You see a phone on a map with satellite signals. A spoofer slowly drags the fake position. Use survey-style countermeasures to catch it: C/N0 uniformity, clock-jump checks, sudden signal-strength shifts, and cross-checking against inertial drift. Each level is a heist-style round: spoof the player, or detect the spoofer. Pure canvas and JS.
ideas.discussion_why: Whimsical and a bit surprising, since a phone's location can be faked. It has weak fit with betting, though geofencing for sportsbooks is a real tie-in. People may argue about location-spoofing to bet in restricted states, but the Discord debate is limited.
